common_name: Pink Poppet Weigela (Dwarf Pale Pink-Flowered Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Pink Poppet stays far smaller than standard weigela cultivars, making it suitable for tight foundation beds and mixed borders.

directions: Pink Poppet is a genuinely dwarf British-bred weigela selection, forming a dense, rounded mound scarcely a third the size of an unimproved Weigela florida. Funnel-shaped flowers open pale pink with a slightly deeper pink reverse in a heavy late-spring flush along the compact branches, drawing bees and the occasional hummingbird. Its small mature footprint suits rock gardens, container culture, and the front of a mixed border where full-sized weigela cultivars would quickly crowd their neighbors. Grow in full sun for the densest flowering and prune lightly right after bloom, since flower buds form on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Victoria needs strong light to hold its darkest foliage color, fading toward green in heavier shade.

directions: Victoria is a long-grown European weigela selection valued for foliage that emerges deep bronze-purple and holds much of that dark coloring through summer, well before the more recent wave of purple-leaved cultivars like Wine and Roses arrived on the market. Clusters of rose-pink, trumpet-shaped flowers open in a heavy late-spring flush against the dark leaves, giving strong two-tone contrast in a mixed shrub border. It grows into a rounded, medium-sized shrub, larger than most modern dwarf purple weigelas, and tolerates average garden soil and summer heat without complaint. Prune immediately after flowering to shape it, since bloom forms on the prior season's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Purpurea is the old-line purple-leaved weigela that many modern dark-foliage cultivars trace back to.

directions: Purpurea is one of the earliest widely distributed purple-leaved weigela selections, carrying dusky maroon-purple new growth that mellows toward bronze-green as the leaves mature through summer. Funnel-shaped, rose-pink flowers open in a heavy late-spring flush against the tinted foliage, giving a softer, more muted color echo than the near-black leaves of newer introductions bred from it. Its compact, rounded habit is smaller than unimproved Weigela florida, fitting readily into a mixed shrub border or foundation planting. Grow in full sun for the strongest foliage color and prune right after flowering, since it blooms on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in light partial shade; some afternoon shelter keeps the golden foliage of Looymansii Aurea from scorching in hot climates.

directions: Looymansii Aurea is an old Dutch weigela selection grown chiefly for its soft golden-yellow foliage, which holds its color best with a little relief from the hottest midday sun rather than in baking full exposure. Funnel-shaped, soft pink flowers open in a late-spring flush against the pale leaves, a gentler pairing than the strong contrast of purple-leaved weigela cultivars. It grows into a medium to large, arching shrub useful as a bright foliage accent or background plant in a mixed border. Water during dry spells in its first couple of seasons, and prune right after flowering to shape it, since bloom forms on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Arnold Giant carries the largest individual flowers of the classic intermedia forsythia selections.

directions: Selected at the Arnold Arboretum, Arnold Giant produces individual flowers noticeably larger than those of Lynwood Gold and other classic border forsythia cultivars, opening bright golden-yellow along bare stems in earliest spring ahead of the foliage. Its habit is looser and more spreading than the tightly upright Lynwood Gold, arching wide enough to need more room in a shrub border or as an informal, large-scale screen. It tolerates a broad range of well-drained soils and is otherwise as trouble-free as any other forsythia. Prune immediately after flowering, cutting the oldest stems back to the ground every few years to keep the naturally sprawling habit from becoming congested, since bloom forms on the previous year's wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
